A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PhoniTale system and experiments. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–D are readable and support comparison, including matching material across the expanded appendix.

before.justification: v2 reports original module-validation results, automated mnemonic comparisons, ablations, and a 51-participant study of recall and preference.

after.justification: v3 retains the work's original automated evaluations, ablations, and 51-participant recall and preference results.

M1.justification: The LSTM transliteration and segmentation models, losses, structural matching algorithm, two-segment constraint, and cue-generation procedure remain unchanged. The added segmentation example and keyword-pool description document the existing approach without establishing a procedural change.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same English–Korean vocabulary-learning setting, 2,870 training pairs, and 36-word evaluation set. Additional languages and code-switched speech recognition appear only as future proposals, not evaluated coverage.

E2.justification: The KSS and OGR comparisons retain the same methods. The cosine-only matching comparison, OGR prompt ablation, and EXAONE3.5 versus GPT-4o ablation also retain their comparators. Newly cited Kanji research is not evaluated.

E3.justification: Table 15 revises the reported KSS evaluation materials, including replacing English or mixed-form anchors with Korean meanings: refurbish's 're' becomes Korean 'again'. Metrics, participant counts, word coverage, and study procedures remain unchanged. These are revisions to reported stimuli; the PDFs do not establish that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The structural-adjustment ablation, prompt and model ablations, attention-map analysis, per-word correctness plot, and case-comparison tables are retained. The expanded cultural explanation of the existing felon example changes interpretation without adding a new tested comparison.

E5.justification: Both versions retain standard-error bars in Figure 3, standard deviations in Table 4, and the same significance statements and participant-equivalence statistics. No new repeated-run information or uncertainty-estimation procedure is reported.

E6.justification: Tables 1–4 and Figures 3 and 10 retain their numerical results. However, Section 4.3's printed autopsy transliteration acquires an extra /s/, despite Figure 2 remaining unchanged. Section 6.5.3 also newly states a preference advantage for KSS's felon cue without supplying its word-level rating.

T1.justification: The problem definitions, loss equations, similarity function, segmentation scoring, and Algorithm 1 retain their mathematical substance. Neither version introduces theoretical propositions or proofs; the added segmentation example is explanatory.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains phonologically guided keyword retrieval combined with LLM-generated cues. Superiority over OGR and recall comparable to human mnemonics were already claimed in v2's conclusion; v3 foregrounds these findings in the abstract. The proposed additional applications remain future work.

C2.justification: KSS's advantage is reinterpreted through cultural familiarity and nonstandard grammar, replacing the emphasis on inflectional flexibility. v3 adds a morpheme-disambiguation explanation and revises the dictionary limitation to acknowledge some conjugated forms while identifying missing everyday vocabulary. Future-work discussion adds specific language adaptations and proposed code-switched speech recognition.

D1.justification: v3 newly specifies the 55,316-entry keyword pool and filtering rules, names the English training-IPA source, explains syllable-boundary annotation, and discloses GPT-4o temperature 0.7 for both OGR and PHT. These additions clarify the existing implementation and evaluation setup without demonstrating changed runs.

R1.justification: v3 adds Lee et al. (2025) on Kanji mnemonics, alongside OpenAI, Oxford, and Pastore references. The abstract shifts its stated research gap toward direct IPA matching and insufficient phonological guidance. The relationship to the principal prior mnemonic methods remains substantially intact.

P1.justification: English translations are added throughout the generation and evaluation prompts, all three 36-word mnemonic tables, and qualitative comparison tables. Together with rewritten abstract, dataset, case-study, and future-work passages, this substantially expands the exposition and accessibility, although the section hierarchy largely remains.

P2.justification: Figures 1 and 4 are retouched, including Figure 1's final segment label changing from S2 to Sn. Best-result entries gain bold formatting, and bilingual appendix tables change column widths, row heights, and placement. The existing display structures and empirical graphics are retained.

improvement.justification: v3 improves auditability through explicit keyword-pool construction, annotation details, generation temperature, and English translations of existing prompts and mnemonic materials. These help readers inspect the retained experiments. The gains are limited by unexplained revisions to the reported KSS stimuli and the newly inconsistent autopsy transcription relative to Figure 2.
